text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- A new report from social authorites reveal the new poor in Sweden -- some 1.7 million people who are unemployed or are in and out of the job market.

- Support for the Swedish government's informal cooperation partner the Centre Party has falled further with only five percent of those surveyed saying they would vote for the party. Support for the conservative Moderate Party is steady at 32 percent and for the ruling Social Democrats, 34 percent compared to 31.5 percent in an April survey.
- Carl Bildt, leader of the conservative party, is considered more knowlegeable, reliable, inspiring and more of a leader than Prime Minister Goran Persson, a poll shows.
- The trend continues -- foreigners were net sellers of Swedish shares in April. So far this year foreigners have sold shares for 11.9 billion crowns net, Riksbank statistics show.

- Some 5,000 plates were placed below a central Stockholm statue on Thursday to represent the Swedish capital's homeless population. In the 1990s the situation for the country's poor has worsened, in part because the number of people who failed to enter the job market rose by 50 percent between 1990 and 1994.
- Swedish-U.S. drugs company Pharmacia & Upjohn is in advanced talks with British Amersham regarding merging its Biotech subsidiary.
- Shares in construction company Skanska fell on Thursday on news the company would have to pay capital gains tax, totalling 2.6 billion crowns, on the sale of a stake in Sandvik.

- The former president of Swedish insurance company Skandia, Bjorn Wolrath, says he believes Skandia will sell off its 15 million share stake in Swedish Match this year. "The investment can not be defended from either an ethical or a financial perspective," Wolrath was quoted as saying.
- Shipping company Frontline is still interested in taking over rival ICB Shipping despite an unsuccessful advance by Frontline, whose major owner is Norwegian John Fredriksen.

- North Atlantic Natural Resources seeks to raise 200 million crowns with a new share issue. The company plans to devote five years to prospecting gold in the area which stretches over Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia.
